title: Guided Project: Test-Driven Development with JUnit 5 in IntelliJ IDEA
subtitle: Build a shopping basket with an offer and a discount code test-first, in short red-green-refactor cycles, with JUnit 5 and IntelliJ IDEA.
outcomes: Work in red-green-refactor cycles: a failing test first, then the simplest code that passes it, then a clean-up
Let IntelliJ IDEA create classes and methods from the failing tests that use them
Write focused JUnit 5 tests, including parameterised tests and tests that expect exceptions
Refactor with your tests as a safety net, using IntelliJ IDEA's automated refactorings
prerequisites: Some Java (classes, methods, lists and maps) and the basics of JUnit 5, as a beginner Java course teaches them. IntelliJ IDEA (the free version is enough) and a JDK of version 21 or later, which IntelliJ IDEA can download for you; Maven comes with IntelliJ IDEA.
description: In this guided project you'll build a small but realistic piece of software, a shopping basket with a buy-three-pay-for-two offer and a discount code, entirely test-first. You'll write each test before the code that makes it pass, watch it fail, make it pass with the simplest code you can, and then tidy up with the tests protecting you: the red-green-refactor cycle of test-driven development. IntelliJ IDEA does much of the typing, creating classes and methods from the tests that use them and refactoring safely. Three short lessons explain the cycle and the habits that make it work; then the lab takes you through the basket one cycle at a time, to a suite of passing JUnit 5 tests that you submit for your instructor's review.

modules.title: Build a shopping basket test-first
modules.summary: Learn the red-green-refactor cycle and how to choose, write and refactor tests, then build a Basket class test-first with JUnit 5 in IntelliJ IDEA.

lessons.title: The red-green-refactor cycle
objectives: Describe the three steps of test-driven development
Explain why a test should fail before you make it pass
key_points: Test-driven development (TDD) means writing a failing test before the code that makes it pass, in short cycles that each take a few minutes.
Red: write one small test for the next piece of behaviour and run it to watch it fail. A test that has never failed might not be testing anything, and a test that doesn't compile counts as failing.
Green: write the simplest code that makes the test pass, even if it looks naive; the next tests push the code towards the general solution.
Refactor: with every test passing, improve the code and the tests, such as names, duplication and structure, without changing what they do, and run the tests after each change.
Writing the test first means using a class before it exists, so its methods are designed from the point of view of the code that calls them.

steps.do: Download the lab's starter project, open it with File | Open (choose the folder that holds pom.xml) and open BasketTest in src/test/java/org/example/basket.
Write a Basket field, a @BeforeEach method and the first test. Basket doesn't exist yet.
steps.see: Basket is red. The test doesn't compile, which counts as failing.

steps.do: Put the caret on Basket, open Show Context Actions and choose Create class 'Basket'. If IntelliJ IDEA asks where to put it, choose src/main/java, so that it's production code rather than test code.
Back in the test, put the caret on totalInCents, open Show Context Actions and choose to create the method in Basket. Make sure it returns an int.
Run the test with the arrow beside it.
steps.see: Green: an empty basket's total is 0.

steps.do: Red again: write the next test, then create add(Item) in Basket from it with Show Context Actions.
Run the tests.
steps.see: The new test fails with expected: <250> but was: <0>.

steps.do: Green: make it pass with the simplest code, such as adding the item's price to a total field, and rerun the tests.
Refactor: rename anything that doesn't read well, then rerun the tests to stay green.

lessons.title: Choosing and writing good tests
objectives: Choose the next test so that each step is small
Write tests that are fast, independent and easy to read
key_points: Pick the next test as the smallest step the code can't do yet: start with the simplest cases, such as an empty basket and one item, before combinations and edge cases.
Good unit tests are fast, repeatable and independent of each other and of the order they run in, and each checks one behaviour, so a failure points straight at the cause.
Name each test after the behaviour it checks, such as threeForTwoMakesEveryThirdUnitFree, and lay it out as arrange, act, assert.
Test rules at their boundaries: for a code that needs a total of at least 2000 cents, test 1990 and 2000 as well as a typical total.
Let tests drive validation too: a test that expects IllegalArgumentException for a quantity of zero is what makes you write the check.

walkthrough.title: Make tests quick to write and read

steps.do: Turn tests that differ only in their data into one parameterised test.
ParameterizedTest and ValueSource are red until they're imported: put the caret on each and open Show Context Actions to add the import.
Run every test in the class with the arrow beside the class name.
steps.see: One entry per value under quantityMustBeAtLeastOne, numbered [1] and [2].

steps.do: After a failure, click Rerun Failed Tests in the Run tool window to run only the tests that failed.
Jump between BasketTest and Basket.
See every test in the class at a glance in the file structure popup.

lessons.title: Refactoring under green tests
objectives: Decide when to refactor, and when to stop
Refactor safely with IntelliJ IDEA's automated refactorings
key_points: Refactor only when every test passes, in small steps, running the tests after each one. If a test goes red, undo the last step rather than debugging it.
Typical refactorings give things better names, extract a method or a constant from an unclear expression, and remove duplication, in the tests as well as in the code.
Money is usually held as whole cents in an int or a long, or as a BigDecimal, rather than as a double, which can't hold most decimal fractions exactly: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004.
IntelliJ IDEA's automated refactorings change every reference at once, so the code keeps compiling and the tests keep meaning the same thing.
Stop refactoring when the code says clearly what it does and repeats nothing; leave further clean-ups until a new test needs them.

steps.do: Run the tests first, so you know they all pass before you change anything.
Give a magic number a name: select 2000 and extract a constant, such as MIN_TOTAL_FOR_CODE.
Extract part of a long method, such as working out how many units an offer makes free, into a method of its own.
Inline a variable whose name adds nothing.
Open Refactor This to see every refactoring available at the caret.
Rerun the tests after each step.
If a change goes wrong, right-click the file and choose Local History | Show History to see and restore an earlier version.

lab.title: Build a shopping basket test-first
lab.goal: Build a Basket class test-first, one red-green-refactor cycle at a time: items and quantities, removing items, a buy-three-pay-for-two offer, a ten per cent discount code and input validation, ending with a suite of passing JUnit 5 tests.
setup: IntelliJ IDEA (the free version is enough) and a JDK of version 21 or later
The starter project: pom.xml, Item.java and BasketTest.java, in the folders shown

steps.do: Open the starter project with File | Open, choosing the folder that holds pom.xml, and trust it. Read Item.java: an item has a SKU, a name and a price in whole cents, so 250 means 2.50.
Cycle 1, red: in BasketTest, add the basket field, setUp and newBasketIsEmpty. Create Basket (in src/main/java) and totalInCents from the test with Show Context Actions.
Green: make totalInCents return 0 and run the test.
Cycles 2 to 4: add these tests one at a time. Run each one and watch it fail before you write the code that makes it pass, then run all the tests.
Cycles 5 to 7: quantities of the same item, removing an item, and removing one that isn't there. Add quantityOf(String sku) and remove(String sku).
Cycle 8: a quantity must be at least 1. Add the parameterised test, using Show Context Actions to import ParameterizedTest and ValueSource.
Refactor: extract the price-times-quantity calculation into a method, and rerun the tests.
Cycle 9: the buy-three-pay-for-two offer. Add the test, then threeForTwo(String sku), and the saving in totalInCents: for an item on the offer, quantity / 3 of its units are free.
Cycle 10, your own test: an offer applies only to its own item. Put TEA on the offer, add three CAKEs and expect 1200.

Cycles 11 to 13, your own tests, for applyCode("SAVE10"), which takes 10% off the total: two JAMs (2500) cost 2250; a @CsvSource test that adds new Item("GIFT", "Gift card", total) shows that 1990 stays 1990 but 2000 becomes 1800; and 2345 becomes 2111, because the discount is rounded down to whole cents.

Cycles 14 and 15, your own tests: offers apply before the code, so three JAMs on the offer plus one TEA (2750 after the offer) cost 2475; and the code's minimum looks at the total after offers, so nine TEAs on the offer stay at 1500.
Cycle 16, your own test: any code other than SAVE10 throws IllegalArgumentException.

Refactor the whole class with the tests green: clear names, no repeated calculations, and constants for 2000 and 10. Then run the tests with coverage (Run with Coverage, from the gutter arrow's menu) and check that every line of Basket ran.
Run the whole suite with Maven: double-click Lifecycle | test in the Maven tool window.
steps.see: Tests run: 23, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, then BUILD SUCCESS.

checks.text: Every test passes in Maven's build.
The offer is tested with a parameterised test and makes every third unit of its own item free, and only that item's.
The discount code is tested at its boundaries, 1990 and 2000, and the rounding down of 2345 to 2111.
Tests that expect exceptions drive the validation: a quantity below 1, removing a missing item and an unknown code.
Basket is tidy after refactoring, with named constants instead of magic numbers.

lab.submit: Paste Basket.java and BasketTest.java, the Tests run line and result from the Maven test build, and two or three sentences about one cycle: the failing test, the simplest code that passed it, and what you refactored afterwards.
hints: If a new test passes straight away, check that it tests something new: a test should fail before you write its code.
With ints, quantity / 3 is the number of free units on a buy-three-pay-for-two offer: 7 / 3 is 2.
Integer division also rounds the discount down: total * 10 / 100 is 234 when the total is 2345.
A LinkedHashMap<String, Integer> of quantities by SKU, with a Map<String, Item> of the items, is one simple way to hold the basket.
